newsitem.title: JAPAN: US may pressure dlr if Japan demand falls - Goldman.
newsitem.headline: US may pressure dlr if Japan demand falls - Goldman.

text.p: New pressure by U.S. authorities for a weaker dollar may emerge if Japan's domestic demand declines, Goldman Sachs International managing director and chief currency economist Jim O'Neill said in Tokyo on Tuesday.

As long as Japan's domestic demand continues to recover, U.S. exporters can maintain their competitiveness at an exchange rate of 110 yen to the dollar, and the yen could stay weak, O'Neill told a seminar on the outlook for major currencies, sponsored by Goldman Sachs.

But given declining Japanese imports and rising exports, and Japan's shift in fiscal policy from expansion to tightening, new pressure from the U.S. side might emerge and the yen would no longer stay weak, he said.
Almost all major currencies were staying at their theoretical price against the dollar at present, O'Neill said.
He forecast that the dollar would start weakening against the yen in early 1997 to 105 yen on a six-month horizon.
The mark's rate against the yen would decline to 70 yen on a six-month basis, and the Swiss franc would depreciate by 10 percent against the yen over the same period.

He said one of the best strategies was to buy yen and sell Swiss francs next year. Switzerland was suffering from low economic growth and the situation there was just as it had been 18 months ago in Japan.
In the "dollar block", the Canadian dollar was the most attractive, despite relatively low interest rates there, he said.
O'Neill said the Italian lira's strength was about to end, although it was expected to stay strong for a little while.
European Union finance ministers agreed on Sunday to bring the lira back into the exchange rate mechanism (ERM) at 990 per mark after it moved out of the mechanism in 1992.
He also recommended purchases of a basket of high-yielding currencies of emerging market nations.
